chapter_theme: Worship of Siva in his devotees (மகேசுவர பூசை): what is given to the devotee, the walking temple, reaches the god, and feeding one knower of Siva outweighs gifts to thousands of Brahmins and the building of temples.
structure_note: The thesis comes first (1857): gifts to the living devotee reach the god in the temple, not the reverse. The rest ranks feeding the devotee above ritual gifts (1858 to 1861, 1866), praises the ash-wearing devotees (1862, 1864), turns briefly to the poet's own devotion (1863) and to false worshippers (1865), and ends on charity to ascetics as the end of karma (1867).

1857.reading: If you give something to the god of the temple of images, it does not reach the Lord in the walking temple; if you give something to the Lord in the walking temple, it reaches the god of the temple of images.
1857.nuance: படமாடக் கோயில் is the built temple with its images (படம் may also be its banners); நடமாடக் கோயில் is the living devotee, whose body houses the Lord. The verse does not forbid temple offerings; it says they flow one way only.

1858.reading: What the ascetics of steady mind eat with delight, the three worlds have eaten, and what they receive, the three worlds have received: so Nandi of the eight directions declared.
1858.nuance: தண்டு அறு சிந்தை is a mind without obstruction or wavering. The claim is that feeding one such ascetic feeds the whole world, and it is given Nandi's authority.

1859.reading: A rare gift made to the realised one who stays settled in a single measure becomes holy water for the three gods and for the thrice seven elders; understand this.
1859.nuance: ஆத்தன் is taken as the trustworthy, realised one. மாத்திரை ஒன்றினில் may be one moment, one measure of breath, or one syllable. மூவேழ் குரவர் is commonly read as twenty-one generations of forebears whom the gift sanctifies.

1860.reading: What if one gives a thousand villages to Brahmins, what if one builds a thousand temple towers? Nothing equals the merit of giving a midday meal to a jnani; that is certain.
1860.nuance: அகரம் is the agraharam, a village granted to Brahmins, and சிகரம் the tower of a temple: the two great religious gifts of a king, both set below one meal.

1861.reading: Feeding ten million Brahmins learned in the rare Veda who perform the six duties does not bring the fruit of thinking of the ash-wearing servant of the Lord; if it is gain one wants, a single handful given to him is the gain.
1861.nuance: ஆறிடும் வேள்வி is taken as the Brahmin's six duties (studying and teaching, sacrificing and having sacrifice done, giving and receiving). The syntax of line 3 is compressed; the sense of comparison is clear but the exact construction is not.

1862.reading: Those who wear the ash crying 'Lord who rides the bull, our master' are devotees, gods walking on earth; those who honour them apart, saying 'this is the Lord with the river on his red locks', have no karma.
1862.nuance: வேறு அணிவார் is unclear: those who honour the devotees specially, or who adorn them as the Lord. Either way the verse treats seeing the Lord in his devotees as what frees from karma.

1863.reading: Glorious Nandi took me and sent me as his holy word; until I come back, though I ache and ache, I will not stop babbling 'Great Nandi' of the one with shining matted hair.
1863.nuance: திருமுகம் can be a royal letter or the holy face. On the first reading Tirumular is Nandi's message sent into the world, which fits the tradition that he was sent south from Kailasa.

1864.reading: By worshipping Hara's devotees, who know no decline, the world's thick darkness leaves; seeking the gracious one so as not to fall short, and rising after worship, there is a joy unlike any on earth.
1864.nuance: பண்பன் (the one of goodness) may be the Lord or the devotee; the verse moves from honouring devotees to seeking him without a break.

1865.reading: Those who worship the Lord without the fitting disposition, entering as if possessed and matching only in outward face, stay deluded within age after age and, for all their inquiry, come to nothing.
1865.nuance: The verse plays on மத்தர் (the frenzied): புகுமத்தர், முகமத்து, அகமத்தர். Its target may be worshippers of the temple image who neglect the devotees, given the chapter's argument, but the verse does not say so.

1866.reading: The food eaten by those in the wise guise of devotees is as if the Father, Brahma and Vishnu had eaten it; if the clear-minded drink what they leave, it is release: so our Mulan has said.
1866.nuance: ஊன் here is food, not flesh. சேடம் is the remnant of the devotee's meal, which tradition treats as sanctified. Tirumular names himself (நம் மூலன்) as the authority.

1867.reading: Those who never fall still strive at rare austerity; charity done to them alone sinks deep karma, removes it along with hard and cleaving karma, and becomes the golden world.
1867.nuance: The kinds of karma (ஆழ்வினை, அருவினை, போழ்வினை) are not clearly distinguished; the repetition may be for sound. The subject of தீர்க்கும் may be the charity or the ascetics.

links.note: 1823 makes the body a temple and the soul a Siva-linga; 1857 draws the consequence for giving: the devotee is a walking temple, and what he receives reaches the god of the built one.
Both rank feeding a jnani above the great religious gifts; 1851 by multiples of merit, 1860 against a thousand villages and a thousand temple towers.
Both set one simple act above a thousand great rites: the Kural puts not killing and eating above a thousand sacrifices, Tirumular puts one meal for a jnani above a thousand gifts to Brahmins.
The Kural sees householders as those who provide for renunciants, perhaps at the cost of their own austerity; Tirumular makes that provision the highest merit, above feeding Brahmins.
1858 says what the ascetic eats the three worlds eat; 1866 says the three gods eat it, and adds that his leavings give release.

Tirumanthiram 1829 says the Lord bathes in the nine holy waters when one washes the feet of those high in true knowledge. 1859 says a gift made to the realised one (ஆத்தனுக்கு ஈந்த) becomes holy water (தீர்த்தமதாம்) for the three gods and the forebears. Both move the sacred waters from the river to the service of the realised person, by washing in 1829 and by giving in 1859.

Tirumanthiram 1857 says what is given to the walking temple (நடமாடக் கோயில்), the devotee, reaches the god of the built temple. 1862 calls the ash-wearing devotees gods walking on earth (நிகழ் தேவர்கள்) and says those who honour them as the Lord himself have no karma. Both see the Lord in the living devotee; 1857 states where offerings go, 1862 what honouring the devotee earns.

Tirumanthiram 2626 says no one can speak of the Lord unless they come to share in the devotion of his devotees (பத்தர்தம் பத்தியிற் பாற்படில் அல்லது). 1864 says that by worshipping Hara's devotees (அரன் அடியாரைத் தொழுகை) the world's thick darkness leaves, and rising after worship there is joy. 1864 extends 2626's claim from knowing the Lord to the whole world's darkness and the worshipper's joy.

Kural 278 says many go about concealed, bathing as if great while their minds are defiled (மனத்தது மாசாக). Tirumanthiram 1865 says those who worship without the fitting disposition, matching only in outward face (முகமத்தோடு ஒத்து), stay deluded within (அகமத்தர்) age after age. Both set a correct outward rite against an inner state that does not match it; the Kural names the defiled mind, Tirumular the frenzy that passes for devotion.

Kural 263 asks whether others have forgotten tapas in order to provide for those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). Tirumanthiram 1867 says that charity done to those who never fall still and strive at rare austerity (அருந்தவம்) removes deep karma and becomes the golden world. The Kural observes that householders serve renunciants in place of their own tapas; Tirumular names what that service gains them.

source_issues: 1864: line 2 reads தூfங்கிருள், with a stray Latin letter; read தூங்கிருள். தொழுகை may be a misprint for தொழுக.
1865: the verse is obscure and its last line (ஆய்ந்தொழிந் தா ரே) is split oddly; the text may be corrupt.
